dossier.public_summary: The dip changes depth by a factor of two between sectors and between transits, with one very deep transit driving the signal. That is not expected for a planet around the target, but matches a blended eclipse from a nearby star picked up differently in different apertures. The on-target centroid is inconclusive, so the best explanation is a false positive, not a planet.

reasons.why: Depths differ dramatically between sectors: sector 58 501±172 ppm vs sector 85 2066±181 ppm. sector_depths_by_source returns changes_within_a_source with p_constant_all 3.6623906363637853e-10, so the change is real, not a calibration offset. A planet transiting the target should have a steady (diluted) depth; factor ~2 change is expected when different apertures pick up different amounts of a blended neighbour's eclipse.
Individual transit depths are inconsistent. One epoch is far deeper than the others and carries most of the signal, inconsistent with a stable planet transit on the target.

reasons.why: No on-target centroid, leaving a neighbour plausible. With 23 stars that could cause a ~1335 ppm dip and centroid inconclusive, the variable-depth, outlier-driven signal is best explained as a false positive, likely a blended eclipsing binary.
